\chapter{The Past Built From Have}
\label{ch:perfekt}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I did in German — haben in second place, the participle waiting at the end of the clause — and read it as a plain past rather than as “have done”.}

The Perfekt is haben plus a participle, and its cost is the four person slots rather than the recipe: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben each get their own lesson before any of them share a page. The bracket that leaves the participle stranded at the end of the clause gets one of its own too, then gestern to fill the gap it opens, and finally the translation trap — ich habe gesagt is “I said”.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[haben plus Partizip]{haben plus a participle — the everyday past}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-perfekt}



\begin{quote}
A participle on its own says nothing about who or when. It needs a partner, and German picks the same partner English does.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the recipe}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{haben}, conjugated for whoever did it, plus the \textbf{participle}.
\end{quote}

That two-part past has a name in German: the \emph{\textbf{Perfekt}}. \emph{Haben} carries everything that changes — the person, and the fact that this is a finished action — while the participle sits there in one shape for everybody. Only one of the two words has to agree with anything, which is why the \emph{Perfekt} costs far less to learn than its size suggests.

English assembled the identical machine out of the identical parts: a verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}have,\textquotedblright{} plus a finished-action participle. \emph{I have said} and \emph{ich habe gesagt} line up word for word. The next few lessons take \emph{haben}'s forms one at a time and hang a participle off each.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the recipe — \textquotedblleft{}haben, conjugated, plus the participle\textquotedblright{}
  \item the name — \textquotedblleft{}das Perfekt\textquotedblright{}
  \item which half moves — \textquotedblleft{}haben changes, the participle does not\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}haben plus participle.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two pieces make the \emph{Perfekt}? (\textbf{Haben} plus the \textbf{participle}.) Which of the two changes for the person? (\emph{\textbf{Haben}}.) Which English tense is built the same way? (\textbf{I have said} — \emph{have} plus a participle.) Next: the first person, and the first whole sentence about the past.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich habe gesagt]{ich habe gesagt — \textquotedblleft{}I said\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-ich-habe-gesagt}



\begin{quote}
The recipe, filled in for the person you talk about most.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ich habe gesagt}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich habe gesagt} — \textquotedblleft{}I said.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three words, three jobs. \emph{Ich} is who; \emph{habe} is the form of \emph{haben} that goes with \emph{ich}; \emph{gesagt} is what happened. Nothing here is new except the way the last two sit together.

Say it as one run rather than three separate words. The stress lands on \emph{gesagt}, and \emph{habe} shrinks in ordinary speech to something close to \emph{hab}: \emph{ich HAB gezahkt}. That contraction is not sloppy — it is how the sentence sounds when a German says it at speed.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ich-laut} — \emph{ich} still ends in the soft breathy sound from the very first chapter, not a \emph{k}.
  \item \texttt{ge-prefix} — and the \emph{ge-} that follows two words later is just as soft. The sentence has two unstressed mumbles in it and one loud syllable.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item it at speed — \textquotedblleft{}ich hab gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English beside it — \textquotedblleft{}I said; ich habe gesagt\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gesagt, ich habe gesagt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I said.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich habe gesagt}.) Which word carries the person? (\emph{\textbf{Habe}}.) Which syllable is stressed? (\emph{\textbf{Sagt}}.) Next: the same sentence, aimed at the person in front of you.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[du hast gesagt]{du hast gesagt — \textquotedblleft{}you said\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-du-hast-gesagt}



\begin{quote}
Same sentence, different person — and \emph{haben} loses a letter on the way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: du hast gesagt}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{du hast gesagt} — \textquotedblleft{}you said,\textquotedblright{} to one person you are on familiar terms with.
\end{quote}

The \emph{b} of \emph{haben} has gone. Not worn away here and kept elsewhere — this is one of the two forms where German drops it, and you met both when you learned the verb.

English does exactly the same thing to exactly the same verb: \emph{I have}, but \emph{thou ha\textbf{st}}, and still today \emph{he ha\textbf{s}}. Two languages, one shortcut, inherited together rather than invented twice.

The participle has not moved. \emph{Gesagt} is \emph{gesagt} whoever did the saying, so half of every sentence in this chapter is already yours.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}du hast gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gesagt, du hast gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English echo — \textquotedblleft{}du hast, thou hast\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}du hast gesagt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}you said,\textquotedblright{} informally. (\textbf{Du hast gesagt}.) Which letter of \emph{haben} disappeared? (\textbf{The b}.) Which English form does the same? (\emph{\textbf{Thou hast}}, and \emph{he has}.) Did the participle change? (\textbf{No}.) Next: the same sentence about somebody else.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[er hat das gemacht]{er hat das gemacht — \textquotedblleft{}he did that\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-er-hat-gemacht}



\begin{quote}
Third person, and the first sentence in this chapter with a word standing between \emph{haben} and the participle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: er hat das gemacht}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{er hat das gemacht} — \textquotedblleft{}he did that.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Hat} is the second of \emph{haben}'s two \emph{b}-less forms, the twin of English \emph{has}. And \emph{das}, the little word you met as an article, doubles as \textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{} — the thing he did.

Notice where it went. \emph{Das} did not follow \emph{gemacht}; it slipped in \textbf{before} it. The participle stayed at the far end of the sentence and let the rest of the words file in ahead of it. That is not a quirk of this one sentence, and the next lesson but one is about it.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ch-ach} — the throat scrape is back, in the middle of \emph{gemacht}.
  \item \texttt{final-t} — three of the four words in this sentence end in a \emph{t}. Release each one; German does not let a final \emph{t} go soft.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}er hat das gemacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item the b-less pair — \textquotedblleft{}du hast, er hat\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the other participle — \textquotedblleft{}er hat das gesagt\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}er hat das gemacht.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}he did that.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Er hat das gemacht}.) Which two forms of \emph{haben} have no \emph{b}? (\emph{\textbf{Hast}} and \emph{\textbf{hat}}.) Where did \emph{das} land — before or after the participle? (\textbf{Before}.) Next: the same past, said about a group.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wir haben gesagt]{wir haben gesagt — \textquotedblleft{}we said\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-wir-haben-gesagt}



\begin{quote}
The fourth person, and the easiest of the four, because its form is one you have been saying since the verb was introduced.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: wir haben gesagt}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{wir haben gesagt} — \textquotedblleft{}we said.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The helper here is \emph{haben} itself, unchanged from the dictionary form. German does that everywhere: the \emph{wir} form of any verb is the infinitive over again, which is one of the few completely free pieces of the ending system.

So the sentence has \emph{haben} in it twice over in a sense — as the recipe's helper and as its own plain shape — and the participle at the back is still \emph{gesagt}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir haben gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four helpers in order — \textquotedblleft{}habe, hast, hat, haben\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir haben das gemacht\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}wir haben gesagt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}we said.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Wir haben gesagt}.) Which other form of the verb does \emph{wir haben} match exactly? (\textbf{The infinitive}, \emph{haben}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}we did that.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Wir haben das gemacht}.) Next: why the participle keeps ending up at the back.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[das Partizip am Ende]{The participle waits at the back}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-partizip-am-ende}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Er hat das gemacht.} Something happened in that sentence that has not been named yet, and it is the one thing about the \emph{Perfekt} English cannot copy.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where the participle goes}]
\begin{quote}
The participle goes to the \textbf{end of the clause}, not next to \emph{haben}.
\end{quote}

You already know that the working verb takes the second position in a German sentence. The \emph{Perfekt} splits the verb in two and puts the halves at opposite ends: \emph{haben} in its usual second slot, the participle at the very back. Between them sits everything else the sentence has to say.

Grammarians call that shape a \textbf{bracket}, and once you hear it you cannot unhear it — a German sentence opens a verb and does not close it until the last word. It is also why German listeners wait: until the bracket shuts, you do not yet know what was done.

English refuses this outright. \emph{I have German learned} is not a sentence, and no amount of context rescues it, because English keeps its two verb pieces welded together and pushes everything else behind them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the shape — \textquotedblleft{}haben second, participle last\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}er hat das gemacht\textquotedblright{} and hear the bracket close
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir haben das gesagt\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}The participle waits at the back.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the participle sit? (\textbf{At the end of the clause}.) Where does \emph{haben} sit? (\textbf{Second}, as any working verb does.) What is between them? (\textbf{Everything else}.) Can English do this? (\textbf{No}.) Next: a word to put in that middle space.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gestern]{gestern — \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-gestern}



\begin{quote}
The bracket leaves a gap in the middle of every past sentence. Here is the first word worth putting in it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: gestern}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{gestern} — \textquotedblleft{}yesterday.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It pairs with \emph{morgen}, which you already have for \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow.\textquotedblright{} One word each side of today, and both of them slide into the middle of a sentence rather than onto its end.

Now put it to work with a participle you own:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt.} \emph{(word for word: I have yesterday German learned.)}
\end{quote}

Three things stacked between \emph{habe} and \emph{gelernt}, and the participle still waiting at the back. Read the English gloss aloud and hear how badly it fails as an English sentence; that failure is the shape of German.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ge-prefix} — the opening \emph{ge-} is the same unstressed mumble as in a participle, though here it is simply part of the word: \emph{GES-tern}, stress on the first syllable.
  \item \texttt{r-uvular-german} — the \emph{r} before \emph{n} barely sounds; it colours the vowel and gets out of the way.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Gestern} and \emph{yesterday} are the same word. Germanic *\emph{gestra-} meant \textquotedblleft{}the day before\textquotedblright{}; German kept it as it was, and English glued \emph{day} onto the end of it, which is why the English word is two syllables longer for no extra meaning.

Latin took the same ancient root to \emph{heri}, which is where French \emph{hier} and Spanish \emph{ayer} come from — so the word for yesterday is one of the oldest things in the room.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gestern\textquotedblright{} — stress on the front
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}gestern, morgen\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}yesterday.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Gestern}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I learned German yesterday.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt}.) Which word comes last? (\emph{\textbf{Gelernt}}.) Which English word is \emph{gestern}? (\emph{\textbf{Yesterday}}.) Next: what that sentence actually means in English, which is not what it looks like.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich habe gesagt = I said]{It means \textquotedblleft{}I said,\textquotedblright{} not only \textquotedblleft{}I have said\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-perfekt-als-vergangenheit}



\begin{quote}
The last thing about this tense is a translation trap, and it is the one that trips up English speakers hardest.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one German past for two English ones}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Ich habe gesagt}} covers both \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I said}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I have said}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

English keeps those apart and makes the difference do work: \emph{I said it yesterday} against \emph{I have said it already}. Pick the wrong one and an English speaker hears something slightly off.

Spoken German mostly does not bother. The \emph{Perfekt} took over the whole territory and answers both questions, so \emph{ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt} is \textquotedblleft{}I learned German yesterday\textquotedblright{} — plain past, no \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{} anywhere in the English.

That is the trap: the German sentence has a word that looks like \emph{have} in it, and the English translation usually does not. Read the German for its meaning rather than its parts, and the sentence stops sounding stilted.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gesagt — I said\textquotedblright{}
  \item it the other way too — \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gesagt — I have said\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt — I learned German yesterday\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich habe gesagt — I said.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Translate \emph{ich habe gesagt} into plain English. (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I said}.\textquotedblright{}) Does the English need the word \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Usually not}.) Which language keeps \emph{I said} and \emph{I have said} apart? (\textbf{English}.) Next: the whole chapter, said through.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the Perfekt, all four persons}

\label{lesson:GE-C15-perfekt-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Each of the four slots below has had a lesson of its own, so this is the first place it is safe to set them out together.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four slots, assembled}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
ich \textbf{habe} gesagt & I said \\
du \textbf{hast} gesagt & you said \\
er \textbf{hat} gesagt & he said \\
wir \textbf{haben} gesagt & we said \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One half of the sentence moves and the other does not. Run the four aloud and hear that \emph{gesagt} never budges.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Was hast du gestern gemacht?} & What did you do yesterday? \\
\emph{Ich habe Deutsch gelernt.} & I learned German. \\
\emph{Und du?} & And you? \\
\emph{Wir haben das auch gemacht.} & We did that too. \\
\emph{Gut gemacht!} & Well done! \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two joining words slip in without lessons of their own, because the translation carries them: \textbf{was} (\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{auch} (\textquotedblleft{}too\textquotedblright{}). And the last line is already an idiom — \emph{gut gemacht} is exactly English \emph{well done}, participle and all.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four in order — \textquotedblleft{}ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben — gesagt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same four with the other participle — \textquotedblleft{}…gemacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the four helpers without prompting. Say \textquotedblleft{}we did that.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Wir haben das gemacht}.) Where is the participle in every one of those sentences? (\textbf{Last}.) Translate \emph{ich habe gesagt} into plain English. (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I said}.\textquotedblright{}) Next: the other past tense German has, and why you meet it mostly in books.
\end{tcolorbox}
